posts.author: jrburns47
posts.content_md: Whatever it was, it was pretty short, 85 pages, done after 1985. They look like they could be an instructors class notes and pretty basic although gives leads to following up on more sophisticated work. Doesn't match anything in my library. You could probably do as well or better by picking up a used copy of any of Graham Saxby's books published from 1988 onward, variously called "Practical Holography" or "Manual of Practical Holography". Edition four which came out last year is excellent.

posts.author: Din
posts.content_md:
I searched the first part of the url: [http://www2.ensc.sfu.ca](http://www2.ensc.sfu.ca), and came up with a 404, as you see if you follow the link . However, I did find a link to their new site: [http://www.ensc.sfu.ca/](http://www.ensc.sfu.ca/). It's the Simon Fraser School of Engineering. Then I notice that the rest of the url refers to a glennc, So, digging further, we find: [http://www2.ensc.sfu.ca/~glennc/](http://www2.ensc.sfu.ca/~glennc/). Apparently Professor Glenn Chapman wrote the excerpt you link to. You can see that he's largely interested in optics, so he may give a course on it. Anyway, then i looked up the last part of the url:e894. We now find: [https://www.sfu.ca/engineering/faculty- ... apman.html](https://www.sfu.ca/engineering/faculty-and-staff/faculty/glenn_chapman.html), and, if you look at the bottom of the page, you find a course entitled ENSC 894 Special Topics II. I suspect, therefore, Professor Chapman taught holography at Simon Fraser School of Engineering as a special topic, and these are his notes.

His email appears in the link to his page, so perhaps you can ask him directly
